question: God first promise to Abram in Canaan was that He would
option_c: take him to a foreign land
option_d: give the land to his descendants
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **give the land to his descendants**

---

### Explanation:

God’s **first promise** to Abram (later renamed Abraham) in **Canaan** is recorded in **Genesis 12:1–7**. Here’s the key passage:

> **Genesis 12:1–3 (NIV):**  
> *“The Lord had said to Abram, ‘Go from your country, your people and your father’s household to the land I will show you. I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you.’”*

Then, in **Genesis 12:7**, after Abram arrives in Canaan:

> *“The Lord appeared to Abram and said, ‘To your offspring I will give this land.’ So he built an altar there to the Lord, who had appeared to him.”*

---

### Why this is the correct answer:

- While God *did* promise to bless Abram, make him a great nation, and curse those who curse him — **the first specific promise made *in Canaan* was about giving the land to his descendants**.
- The promise of a son (Isaac) comes later, in **Genesis 15** and **17**.
- The command to leave his homeland (to go to a foreign land) was the *call*, not the *promise*.
- The blessing/cursing promise (Genesis 12:3) was given *before* Abram arrived in Canaan — as part of the initial call from Haran.

---

### Therefore:
The **first promise God made to Abram *in Canaan*** was:  
> **“To your offspring I will give this land.”**  
→ **Give the land to his descendants.**

✅ Correct answer: **give the land to his descendants**

question: God blessed and hallowed the seventh day because He
option_a: rested from all his work of creations
option_c: had finished the creation of the heavens
option_d: called all the host of heavens to rest on that day
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **rested from all his work of creation**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to **Genesis 2:2–3**, which says:

> “By the seventh day God had finished the work he had been doing; so on the seventh day he rested from all his work. Then God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all the work of creating that he had done.”  
> *(Genesis 2:2–3, NIV)*

So, God **blessed and hallowed (made holy)** the seventh day **because He rested from all His work of creation**.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **“Declared it a sabbath day”** — While the seventh day *became* the Sabbath, the text doesn’t say God declared it as such *at this point*. The term “Sabbath” (from Hebrew *shabbat*, meaning “to rest”) is applied later in Exodus, but the *reason* for its holiness is rooted in God’s rest after creation.

- **“Had finished the creation of the heavens”** — This is partially true, but incomplete. He finished *all* creation — heavens *and* earth — not just the heavens. The text emphasizes rest from *all* His work.

- **“Called all the host of heavens to rest on that day”** — This is not mentioned in Genesis 2. There’s no indication that angels or heavenly beings were commanded to rest. The focus is on God’s own rest and the sanctification of the day for humanity later.

---

### Key Takeaway:

God’s rest on the seventh day was not due to fatigue, but a deliberate act of completion and blessing. By resting, He modeled the rhythm of work and rest, and set apart the seventh day as holy — a pattern later given to Israel as the Sabbath commandment (Exodus 20:8–11).

✅ So, the best and most accurate answer is: **rested from all his work of creation**.

question: Pharaoh appointed Joseph the overseer of his house for he realized that he was
option_d: full of the spirit of God
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **very trustworthy**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to the biblical story of Joseph in the Book of Genesis (specifically Genesis 39–41). After Joseph was sold into slavery in Egypt, he ended up in the household of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. Joseph proved himself faithful and capable, and Potiphar put him in charge of his entire household.

Later, after Joseph interpreted Pharaoh’s dreams, Pharaoh was so impressed that he appointed Joseph as second-in-command over all of Egypt. Pharaoh said:

> “Since God has shown you all this, there is no one so discerning and wise as you. You shall be in charge of my palace, and all my people are to submit to your orders. Only with respect to the throne will I be greater than you.” — Genesis 41:39–40 (NIV)

Pharaoh’s decision was based on Joseph’s **wisdom, discernment, and proven reliability** — in other words, his **trustworthiness**. Joseph had already demonstrated integrity and competence in Potiphar’s house and later in interpreting dreams and planning for the future.

While Joseph was also “full of the spirit of God” (Genesis 41:38), that phrase describes *why* Pharaoh trusted him — it’s the *reason* for his trustworthiness, not the direct reason for his appointment. The appointment itself was because Pharaoh recognized Joseph as **very trustworthy**.

The other options — “worthy of praise,” “loved by all,” or even “full of the spirit of God” — are not the *primary reason* Pharaoh appointed him. The text emphasizes Joseph’s **reliability and competence**, which made him trustworthy to manage the kingdom.

---

✅ Final Answer: **very trustworthy**

question: The name Moses means
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **drawn out of water**

---

### Explanation:

The name **Moses** comes from the Hebrew name **מֹשֶׁה (Moshe)**. According to the biblical account in **Exodus 2:10**, Pharaoh’s daughter found the baby Moses in a basket among the reeds of the Nile River. She adopted him and named him:

> “**She named him Moses, saying, ‘I drew him out of the water.’**”

The Hebrew root **מָשָׁה (mashah)** means “to draw out” or “to pull out.” So, the name **Moses** literally means **“drawn out of water.”**

This is a direct reference to his rescue from the Nile as an infant — a pivotal moment in his life and in Israelite history.

---

### Why not the others?

- **Baptized in water** — Baptism is a later Christian ritual; not relevant to Moses’ naming.
- **Abandoned in water** — While Moses *was* placed in the water by his mother to save him, the name doesn’t reflect abandonment — it reflects his *rescue*.
- **Washed in water** — No biblical or linguistic basis for this meaning.

---

✅ So, the best and most accurate answer is: **drawn out of water**.

question: Who among the following was to ensure the security of King Saul in the Wilderness of Ziph?
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Abner**

---

### Explanation:

In the biblical narrative, **Abner** was the **commander of King Saul’s army** and his chief military officer. He was responsible for the king’s security and the defense of his realm.

In **1 Samuel 26**, we find the story of David sparing Saul’s life again — this time in the **Wilderness of Ziph**. Saul had come out to hunt David, and David and his men secretly entered Saul’s camp at night. David took Saul’s spear and water jug as proof he could have killed him but chose not to.

Importantly, **Abner** is mentioned in this passage as being responsible for guarding Saul — and David even points out to Abner how he failed in his duty:

> **1 Samuel 26:15–16 (NIV):**  
> “David said to Abner, ‘Don’t you have a sense of duty? You’re supposed to guard the king your master. Someone came to destroy your master the king. What you’ve done is not good. As surely as the Lord lives, you and your men deserve to die, because you did not guard your master, the Lord’s anointed.’”

This clearly shows that **Abner was the one entrusted with Saul’s security**, even in the Wilderness of Ziph.

---

### Why not the others?

- **Joab** — He was David’s nephew and later commander of David’s army, not Saul’s. He was not involved in Saul’s security.
- **Abisha** — Not a known biblical figure in this context. Possibly a confusion with Abishai (David’s brother), but he was on David’s side.
- **Abimelech** — A name associated with Philistine kings (e.g., in Genesis 20 and 26), not an Israelite military officer under Saul.

---

### Final Answer: **Abner** ✅

question: Ishboshet denounced Abner's love for Rizpah because
option_b: Abner did not cooperate with the house of Saul
option_c: he saw in Abner's action a usurpation of his right as heir to the throne
option_d: Abner was in alliance with David
step_by_step:
The correct answer is:  
**he saw in Abner's action a usurpation of his right as heir to the throne**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to a passage in **2 Samuel 3:6–11**, where **Ishboshet** (also called Eshbaal), the son of Saul and the nominal king of Israel after Saul’s death, confronts **Abner**, Saul’s former military commander and a powerful figure in the northern kingdom.

The specific incident occurs when **Abner takes Rizpah**, one of Saul’s concubines. In ancient Near Eastern royal culture, taking a king’s concubine was not merely a personal or sexual matter — it was a **political act** symbolizing a claim to the throne. (See also 2 Samuel 16:20–22, where Absalom does the same to David’s concubines to assert his claim to the kingship.)

When Ishboshet confronts Abner, saying, *“Why have you slept with my father’s concubine?”* (2 Samuel 3:7), he is not just objecting to a personal indiscretion — he is accusing Abner of **acting like a king**, thereby challenging Ishboshet’s own legitimacy as Saul’s heir.

Abner’s response is furious — he essentially says, *“Am I a dog’s head? I’ve been loyal to your father’s house, and now you accuse me of treason?”* (2 Samuel 3:8). He then switches allegiance to David, the rival king of Judah.

---

### Why the other options are incorrect:

- **“Ishboshet hated Abner”** — There’s no textual evidence of personal hatred; the conflict is political.
- **“Abner did not cooperate with the house of Saul”** — Actually, Abner *had* been cooperating — he was the one holding the kingdom together for Saul’s house until this point.
- **“Abner was in alliance with David”** — This happens *after* the confrontation, not before. Ishboshet’s denunciation is what *triggers* Abner’s defection.

---

### Conclusion:

Ishboshet denounced Abner’s relationship with Rizpah because he perceived it as a **symbolic act of royal usurpation** — a challenge to his own position as heir to Saul’s throne. This is a key moment in the power struggle between the houses of Saul and David.

✅ Final Answer: **he saw in Abner's action a usurpation of his right as heir to the throne**

question: Although David was regarded as a man after God's heart, he acted badly before God when he
option_a: refused to slay Saul whom God had totally rejected
option_b: remained at home while his troops were at the battle field
option_c: imprisoned Nathan for condemning his adultery
option_d: commited sins of adultery and murder
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **committed sins of adultery and murder**

---

### Explanation:

David is often referred to in the Bible as “a man after God’s own heart” (1 Samuel 13:14; Acts 13:22). This does not mean he was sinless, but that he had a sincere heart toward God, repenting when he sinned and seeking to follow God’s will.

However, David committed grave sins that deeply displeased God — specifically, **adultery with Bathsheba** and **arranging the murder of her husband, Uriah the Hittite**, to cover up the pregnancy (2 Samuel 11).

This is one of the most significant moral failures in David’s life. The prophet Nathan confronted him with a parable, and when David realized the gravity of his sin, he repented deeply (Psalm 51). God forgave him, but there were still serious consequences — including the death of the child born from the affair and ongoing family turmoil.

---

### Why the other options are incorrect:

- **Refused to slay Saul whom God had totally rejected** — This was actually a *righteous* act. David spared Saul’s life multiple times, even though Saul was trying to kill him, because David respected God’s anointing on Saul (1 Samuel 24, 26). This showed David’s reverence for God’s authority.

- **Remained at home while his troops were at the battlefield** — While this *is* the context in which David committed adultery (2 Samuel 11:1), it’s not the sin itself. The sin was the *adultery and murder*, not merely staying home. Staying home wasn’t inherently wrong — kings didn’t always go to war — but it created the opportunity for sin.

- **Imprisoned Nathan for condemning his adultery** — This is false. David did *not* imprison Nathan. In fact, after Nathan confronted him, David immediately confessed his sin and repented (2 Samuel 12:13). Nathan was a trusted prophet, and David respected his message.

---

### Conclusion:

David’s most serious moral failure before God was **committing sins of adultery and murder**, which is why this is the correct answer. It’s a powerful reminder that even godly people can fall into grave sin — but also that God is merciful to those who repent.

✅ Final Answer: **committed sins of adultery and murder**

question: The sons of Eli who demanded raw meat during sacrifice were condemned for
option_c: treating the Lord's offering with contempt
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **treating the Lord's offering with contempt**

---

### Explanation:

This refers to the story of **Hophni and Phinehas**, the sons of Eli, the high priest, as recorded in **1 Samuel 2:12–17**.

They were priests at Shiloh and were responsible for handling the sacrifices brought by the people. Instead of honoring the Lord’s portion (which was to be burned on the altar as an offering to God), they **demanded raw meat before the fat was burned** — essentially taking the best parts for themselves, even **forcing people to give it to them**.

The key verse is **1 Samuel 2:17**:

> “So the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the Lord, for they treated the Lord’s offering with contempt.”

---

### Why the other options are incorrect or incomplete:

- **Eating raw meat** — While they did take raw meat, the issue wasn’t the rawness itself (some meat was eaten cooked or raw in Israelite practice). The sin was *how* and *why* they took it — disrespecting God’s portion.

- **Taking it by force** — This is true (they used intimidation — 1 Sam 2:13–16), but it’s a *method*, not the *core spiritual offense*. The Bible specifically says they “treated the Lord’s offering with contempt.”

- **Behaving arrogantly before the Lord** — Also true, but again, this is a *symptom* or *attitude* behind their actions. The *theological condemnation* centers on their **disrespect for the sacred offerings** — which is what “treating the Lord’s offering with contempt” captures.

---

### Theological Significance:

In ancient Israel, the sacrificial system was sacred — it was how people approached God, atoned for sin, and expressed gratitude. By **usurping the Lord’s portion** and **disregarding His commands**, Hophni and Phinehas were not just being greedy — they were **profaning the holy**. This is why God pronounced judgment on them and their family (1 Sam 2:27–36).

---

✅ So, the best and most accurate answer is: **treating the Lord's offering with contempt**.

question: The Israelite maid who introduced Naaman to Elisha for healing exhibited
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **charity and faith**

---

### Explanation:

This refers to the story of **Naaman the Syrian**, a commander of the army of the king of Aram, who suffered from leprosy. He was healed by the prophet **Elisha** — but it was an **Israelite maid**, taken captive during a raid, who first suggested that Naaman go to Elisha for healing (2 Kings 5:2–3).

> “**The young girl who had been taken captive from the land of Israel said to her mistress, ‘If only my master were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy.’**” (2 Kings 5:2–3, NIV)

---

### Why “charity and faith”?

- **Charity** — The maid, though a captive and likely in a lowly position, showed kindness and concern for her master’s well-being. She didn’t harbor resentment or wish him harm; instead, she offered a solution to his suffering. This reflects **charity** — selfless love and goodwill toward others, even those who may have wronged you.

- **Faith** — She believed that the prophet Elisha in Israel could heal Naaman. She didn’t just suggest a doctor or a remedy — she pointed to a **prophet of God**, showing her **faith in God’s power** working through Elisha. Her faith was bold, especially since Naaman was a foreigner and a military leader of an enemy nation.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Love and patience** — While there may be elements of love, “patience” isn’t particularly highlighted in her brief but pivotal act.
- **Trust and love** — “Trust” is somewhat implied, but “charity” better captures her selfless act toward her captor.
- **Patience and faith** — Again, patience isn’t emphasized; her action was immediate and proactive.

---

### Conclusion:

The Israelite maid’s act was a beautiful example of **charity** (selfless kindness) and **faith** (belief in God’s power to heal through His prophet). She is often held up as a model of humble faith and compassion.

✅ Final Answer: **charity and faith**

question: The rain which fell after the contest between Elijah and the prophets of Baal shows
option_a: that the forces of nature were at work in bringing rain
option_b: the vindication of Yahweh as the true God
option_c: Elijah as a powerful servant of God
option_d: Elijah's authority over the forces of nature
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **the vindication of Yahweh as the true God**

---

### Explanation:

This event is recorded in **1 Kings 18**, where Elijah challenges the 450 prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel. The challenge: whichever god could send fire to consume a sacrifice would be proven as the true God.

- The prophets of Baal call on their god all day — no answer.
- Elijah then prays to Yahweh, and **fire comes down from heaven**, consuming the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and even the water in the trench.
- The people fall down and declare, “The Lord — he is God! The Lord — he is God!” (1 Kings 18:39).

Then, **Elijah tells King Ahab to eat and drink, for he hears the sound of a heavy rain** (1 Kings 18:41). Elijah goes up to the mountain, prays, and after seven times, a small cloud appears — and then **rain pours down**.

---

### Why “the vindication of Yahweh as the true God”?

The **rain** that follows is not just a meteorological event — it’s **theological**. In the context of ancient Israel, **rain was seen as a sign of God’s favor and covenant faithfulness**. Drought (like the one that had lasted 3.5 years) was a sign of divine judgment (Deuteronomy 28:23–24). So, when rain comes after Elijah’s prayer, it’s **God’s confirmation** that He is the true God — the one who controls nature, blesses His people, and answers prayer.

The rain is the **fulfillment of Elijah’s prophecy** and the **divine response** to the contest — showing that Yahweh not only controls fire (judgment), but also controls water (blessing and life).

---

### Why not the other options?

- **“That the forces of nature were at work...”** — This is too naturalistic and misses the theological point. The text presents the rain as a **miraculous, divine act**, not just “nature working.”
  
- **“Elijah as a powerful servant of God”** — While true, this is secondary. The focus is not on Elijah’s power, but on **Yahweh’s power and authority** being demonstrated *through* Elijah.

- **“Elijah’s authority over the forces of nature”** — Again, this overemphasizes Elijah. The text shows that **Elijah prays**, and **God answers** — it’s Yahweh’s authority, not Elijah’s.

---

### Conclusion:

The rain after the contest is **the divine seal of approval** — proving that **Yahweh alone is God**, and that He alone controls the heavens and the earth. Thus, the best answer is:

> **the vindication of Yahweh as the true God** ✅

question: The Jews ignored Rehum's order to stop he reconstruction of the Temple following an advice from
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Haggai and Zechariah**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to events described in the **Book of Ezra**, particularly **Ezra 5:1–2** and **Ezra 6**, which recount the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.

After the initial attempts to rebuild the Temple (started under Zerubbabel and Joshua), the work was halted due to opposition from local officials — including **Rehum**, a royal official who wrote to King Artaxerxes (Ezra 4:8–24), urging him to stop the reconstruction. The king issued an order to halt the work, and for a time, the rebuilding ceased.

However, **the prophets Haggai and Zechariah** encouraged the people to resume the work, reminding them of God’s will and promises. Their prophetic messages (recorded in the books of Haggai and Zechariah) were instrumental in motivating the Jews to restart the Temple construction **despite Rehum’s order**.

> **Ezra 5:1–2 (NIV):**  
> *“Now Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the prophet, a descendant of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them. Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jozadak set to work to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. And the prophets of God were with them, helping them.”*

So, while **Zerubbabel and Joshua** were the political and priestly leaders who physically led the rebuilding, it was the **prophetic encouragement from Haggai and Zechariah** that inspired the people to defy Rehum’s order and resume construction.

---

### Why not the others?

- **Isaiah and Jeremiah** — These prophets ministered *before* the exile (7th–6th century BCE). They were not alive during the post-exilic period when the Temple was being rebuilt.
- **Jattenai and Darius** — Jattenai was a Persian official who investigated the rebuilding (Ezra 5:6–7), not a source of encouragement. Darius was the Persian king who later *approved* the rebuilding (Ezra 6), but he did not advise the Jews to ignore Rehum’s order — rather, he reversed it after finding Cyrus’s original decree.
  
---

### Final Answer:
✅ **Haggai and Zechariah** — They were the prophets who advised and encouraged the Jews to resume rebuilding the Temple despite Rehum’s order.

question: Zerubbabel's response to the pathetic state of the Jews in Judah was
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **rebuild the temple**

---

### Explanation:

Zerubbabel was a key Jewish leader who returned from Babylonian exile to Judah in the late 6th century BCE, under the decree of Persian King Cyrus the Great (c. 538 BCE). He was a descendant of King David and served as governor of Judah.

At the time, the Jews who had returned were in a “pathetic state” — their homeland was in ruins, the temple in Jerusalem had been destroyed by the Babylonians (586 BCE), and the people were demoralized and struggling to reestablish their community.

Zerubbabel’s primary mission, as recorded in the books of **Ezra** and **Haggai**, was to **rebuild the temple in Jerusalem**. This was not just an architectural project — it was a spiritual and national restoration. The temple symbolized God’s presence among His people and was central to Jewish worship and identity.

- **Haggai 1:1–8** records God’s command through the prophet Haggai to Zerubbabel and the people: “Go up to the mountains and bring wood and build the house, so that I may take pleasure in it and be honored,” says the Lord.
- **Ezra 3:8–13** describes how Zerubbabel led the people in laying the foundation of the temple.
- **Ezra 5–6** recounts how, despite opposition, Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest completed the temple under Persian permission.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Rebuild the walls** — This was done later by **Nehemiah** (5th century BCE), not Zerubbabel.
- **Liberate the people from slavery** — The Jews were no longer slaves; they had been *freed* by Cyrus and allowed to return. Zerubbabel didn’t liberate them — he led them in rebuilding.
- **Teach the Jews God’s commandments** — This was primarily the role of **Ezra the scribe**, who came later and read the Law to the people (Ezra 7–10, Nehemiah 8).

---

### Conclusion:

Zerubbabel’s response to the Jews’ desperate condition was to **rebuild the temple**, restoring their spiritual center and national hope. This act was foundational to the post-exilic Jewish community.

✅ Correct Answer: **rebuild the temple**

question: God told Ezekiel at his commissioning that '... briers and thorns are with you and you sit upon scorpions...
option_a: the land of exile should bring forth briers and thorns
option_b: Ezekiel would sit comfortably on scorpions
option_c: briers, thorns and scorpions would torment him
option_d: his situation would be uncorfortable as he prophesied to unwilling people
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **his situation would be uncomfortable as he prophesied to unwilling people**

---

### Explanation:

This phrase comes from **Ezekiel 2:6**, where God commissions Ezekiel as a prophet to the rebellious house of Israel:

> “And you, son of man, do not be afraid of them, nor be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you and you sit upon scorpions. Do not be afraid of their words or be dismayed at their looks, though they are a rebellious house.” (ESV)

---

### What does it mean?

- **“Briers and thorns”** and **“scorpions”** are **metaphors** — not literal plants or creatures — symbolizing **hostility, danger, and discomfort**.
- God is warning Ezekiel that his mission will be **difficult and unpleasant**, because he is being sent to a people who are **rebellious, stubborn, and resistant to God’s message**.
- Sitting on scorpions is an image of **extreme discomfort and danger** — not literal comfort.
- The point is: **Ezekiel will face hostility and hardship** as he delivers God’s word to a people who don’t want to hear it.

---

### Why the other options are wrong:

- ❌ *“The land of exile should bring forth briers and thorns”* — This misinterprets the metaphor as a literal prophecy about the land’s fertility. It’s about the people’s attitude, not agriculture.
- ❌ *“Ezekiel would sit comfortably on scorpions”* — This is the opposite of the meaning. Scorpions symbolize pain and danger.
- ❌ *“Briers, thorns and scorpions would torment him”* — While close, this focuses too narrowly on physical torment. The emphasis is on the **emotional and spiritual difficulty** of prophesying to a hostile, rebellious audience.

---

### Conclusion:

The phrase is a **vivid metaphor** for the **uncomfortable, dangerous, and challenging mission** God is sending Ezekiel on — **prophesying to an unwilling, rebellious people**. So the best answer is:

> **his situation would be uncomfortable as he prophesied to unwilling people** ✅

question: Hosea called upon his children to plead with their mother to desist from all the following except
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **faithfulness to the covenant**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to **Hosea 2:2–5**, where the prophet Hosea, acting as a symbolic representation of God’s relationship with Israel, calls upon his children to plead with their mother (symbolizing Israel or the northern kingdom) to stop her unfaithfulness.

Here’s the key passage (Hosea 2:2–5, NIV):

> “Plead with your mother, plead—  
> for she is not my wife,  
> and I am not her husband.  
> Let her remove the adulterous look from her face  
> and the unfaithfulness from between her breasts.  
> Otherwise I will strip her naked  
> and make her as bare as on the day she was born;  
> I will make her like a desert,  
> turn her into a parched land,  
> and slay her with thirst.  
> I will not show my love to her children,  
> because they are the children of adultery.  
> Their mother has been unfaithful  
> and has conceived them in disgrace.  
> She said, ‘I will go after my lovers,  
> who give me my food and my water,  
> my wool and my linen,  
> my olive oil and my drink.’  
> Therefore I will block her path with thornbushes;  
> I will wall her in so that she cannot find her way.  
> She will chase after her lovers but not catch them;  
> she will look for them but not find them.  
> Then she will say,  
> ‘I will go back to my husband as at first,  
> for then I was better off than now.’  
> She has not acknowledged that I was the one  
> who gave her the grain, the new wine and oil,  
> who lavished on her the silver and gold—  
> which they used for Baal.  
> Therefore I will take away my grain when it ripens,  
> and my new wine when it is ready.  
> I will take back my wool and my linen,  
> which I gave her to cover her nakedness.  
> So now I will expose her lewdness  
> before the eyes of her lovers;  
> no one will take her out of my hand.  
> I will stop all her celebrations:  
> her yearly festivals, her New Moons, her Sabbaths—  
> all her appointed festivals.  
> I will ruin her vines and her fig trees,  
> which she said were her pay from her lovers;  
> I will make them a thicket,  
> and wild animals will devour them.  
> I will punish her for the days  
> she burned incense to the Baals;  
> she decked herself with rings and jewelry,  
> and went after her lovers,  
> but me she forgot,”  
> declares the Lord.

---

### Key Themes in Hosea 2:

- **Harlotry / Adultery** — This is a central metaphor for Israel’s spiritual unfaithfulness to God (v. 2, 5).
- **Burning incense to Baals** — Explicitly mentioned in v. 13 as something God will punish.
- **Lack of knowledge of God** — Hosea 4:1 says, “There is no faithfulness, no love, no acknowledgment of God in the land,” and Hosea 4:6 says, “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.” So this is also a major theme.
- **Faithfulness to the covenant** — This is **what God wants**, not what Israel is doing. It is the **opposite** of what Hosea is calling Israel to stop. In fact, Hosea is calling Israel to *return* to faithfulness to the covenant.

---

### Therefore:

Hosea calls upon his children to plead with their mother to **desist from**:

- ✅ Harlotry (spiritual adultery)
- ✅ Burning incense to Baals (idolatry)
- ✅ Lack of knowledge of God (ignorance of God’s ways)

But **NOT**:

- ❌ Faithfulness to the covenant — because that’s what God *desires* and *calls Israel back to*. It’s the **goal**, not the sin to be abandoned.

---

### Final Answer: **faithfulness to the covenant** ✅

question: "Then Jonah cried to the Lord from the belly of sheol..." Sheol, here means
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **region of darkness and death**

---

### Explanation:

The verse in question — *“Then Jonah cried to the Lord from the belly of Sheol…”* — comes from **Jonah 2:2** (or 2:1 in some versions). This is part of Jonah’s prayer while he is inside the great fish, after being thrown overboard and swallowed.

In this context, **Sheol** is used **figuratively** to describe the **place of the dead** or the **realm of the departed** — a concept in ancient Hebrew thought representing the abode of the dead, often associated with darkness, silence, and separation from God (see Psalm 6:5; 88:3–12; Isaiah 38:18).

Jonah is not literally in Sheol (the underworld), but he feels as if he is — trapped, near death, cut off from the land of the living, and surrounded by water (which in ancient Near Eastern thought was often associated with chaos and death). So he cries out from “the belly of Sheol” to express his **extreme despair and near-death experience**.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Tempestuous sea** — While Jonah was in the sea, “Sheol” is not a synonym for the sea. The sea is the *setting*, but Sheol is the *metaphorical state* he feels himself in.
  
- **Holy temple of the Lord** — This is the *opposite* of Sheol. The temple represents God’s presence and life; Sheol represents absence and death.

- **Deep sea** — Again, while Jonah is physically in the deep sea, the term “Sheol” here is theological and metaphorical, not geographical. The deep sea is the *location*, but Sheol is the *spiritual condition*.

---

### Conclusion:

**Sheol** in Jonah 2:2 symbolizes **the region of darkness and death** — a poetic and theological expression of Jonah’s feeling of being engulfed by death, even as he is physically inside a fish in the sea. It underscores his desperation and need for divine rescue.

✅ Final Answer: **region of darkness and death**

question: Satan assured Jesus that God would "give his angels charge of you" if he should
option_a: throw himself down from the temple pinnacle
option_c: strike his foot against a stone
option_d: command stones to become leaves of bread
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **throw himself down from the temple pinnacle**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to the **temptation of Jesus in the wilderness**, as recorded in the Gospels — specifically **Matthew 4:5–7** and **Luke 4:9–12**.

In this scene, Satan takes Jesus to the **pinnacle of the temple** and says:

> “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.’” (Matthew 4:6, NIV)

Satan is **quoting Psalm 91:11–12**, but he is **misusing Scripture** to tempt Jesus to **test God’s protection** by performing a dramatic, self-destructive act — jumping from the temple — expecting angels to save him.

Jesus responds by quoting Deuteronomy 6:16:  
> “Do not put the Lord your God to the test.”

---

### Why the other options are incorrect:

- **Fall down and worship him** — This was Satan’s *third* temptation (Matthew 4:8–10), where he offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world if He would worship him. Not related to angels or Psalm 91.

- **Strike his foot against a stone** — This is part of the *quote from Psalm 91* that Satan uses, but it’s not the *action* Jesus is being tempted to do. It’s the *consequence* that won’t happen *if* angels protect Him — so it’s not the correct choice.

- **Command stones to become leaves of bread** — This was the *first* temptation (Matthew 4:3), where Satan told Jesus to turn stones into bread to satisfy His hunger. Again, not related to angels or the temple pinnacle.

---

### Summary:

Satan assured Jesus that God would “give his angels charge of you” **if he should throw himself down from the temple pinnacle** — a tempting but dangerous misuse of Scripture to test God’s protection.

✅ Correct answer: **throw himself down from the temple pinnacle**

question: When Jesus sent out the Twelve, he commanded them to
option_a: preach from house to house and bless the people
option_b: extort, teach, correct and convert everybody
option_c: preach, heal, raise the dead and cast out demons
option_d: preach the gospel and baptise believers
step_by_step:
The correct answer is:  
**- preach, heal, raise the dead and cast out demons**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to the account in the **Gospel of Matthew, chapter 10**, where Jesus sends out the Twelve Apostles on a mission. In **Matthew 10:5–8**, Jesus gives them specific instructions:

> “These twelve Jesus sent out with the following instructions: ‘Do not go among the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans. Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel. As you go, proclaim this message: “The kingdom of heaven has come near.” Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse those who have leprosy, drive out demons. Freely you have received; freely give.’” (NIV)

So, Jesus explicitly commands them to:
- **Preach** (proclaim the message: “The kingdom of heaven has come near”)
- **Heal the sick**
- **Raise the dead**
- **Cast out demons** (also called “drive out demons”)

These are supernatural signs meant to authenticate their message and demonstrate the power of God’s kingdom.

---

### Why the other options are incorrect:

- **“Preach from house to house and bless the people”** — While they were to go from town to town, “house to house” preaching is more associated with later missionary work (e.g., Acts 5:42 or 20:20), not specifically Jesus’ command to the Twelve in Matthew 10.

- **“Extort, teach, correct and convert everybody”** — “Extort” is clearly wrong — Jesus never commanded extortion. Also, “convert everybody” is not the language or intent of Matthew 10; they were sent specifically to “the lost sheep of Israel.”

- **“Preach the gospel and baptise believers”** — This is more aligned with the **Great Commission** in **Matthew 28:19–20**, given *after* Jesus’ resurrection, not the initial sending out of the Twelve.

---

### Conclusion:

The most accurate and biblically supported answer is:  
> **preach, heal, raise the dead and cast out demons**

This reflects Jesus’ direct commission to the Twelve in Matthew 10.

question: When Jesus healed the paralytic, the Scribes accused him of
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **blasphemy**

---

### Explanation:

This event is recorded in the Gospels — specifically **Mark 2:1–12**, **Matthew 9:1–8**, and **Luke 5:17–26**.

Jesus healed a paralytic man who was lowered through the roof by his friends. Before healing him physically, Jesus said:

> **“Son, your sins are forgiven.”** (Mark 2:5)

At this point, **the scribes** (religious teachers of the law) reacted internally:

> **“Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”** (Mark 2:7)

---

### Why “blasphemy”?

- In Jewish theology, **only God has the authority to forgive sins**.
- By declaring the man’s sins forgiven, Jesus was claiming divine authority — something the scribes interpreted as **blasphemy** (speaking irreverently or sacrilegiously about God, or claiming divine prerogatives for oneself).
- Jesus then proved His authority by healing the man — showing that if He could heal the body, He could also forgive sins, which is a spiritual act only God can do.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Self-conceit / Arrogance / Presumption** — While these might describe the scribes’ *perception* of Jesus, they are not the *theological charge* they leveled against Him. The scribes didn’t accuse Him of being merely proud or presumptuous — they accused Him of **blasphemy**, a serious religious offense under Jewish law.

---

### Conclusion:

The scribes accused Jesus of **blasphemy** because they believed only God could forgive sins, and Jesus’ words implied He possessed that divine authority.

✅ Final Answer: **blasphemy**

question: The rich man who ignored the needs of Lazarus lacked
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **human sympathy**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to the **Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus**, found in **Luke 16:19–31** in the Bible. In this story:

- A rich man lives luxuriously every day, dressed in fine clothes and feasting sumptuously.
- At his gate lies a poor man named Lazarus, covered in sores, longing for scraps from the rich man’s table.
- The rich man **ignores Lazarus’s suffering** completely — he doesn’t offer help, comfort, or even basic compassion.
- When both die, Lazarus is taken to Abraham’s side (heaven), while the rich man ends up in torment (hell).

Jesus tells this parable to highlight the moral failure of the rich man — not necessarily his wealth, but his **lack of compassion and empathy** toward a suffering neighbor.

---

### Why “human sympathy”?

- **Human sympathy** means the ability to feel for others, to recognize their pain, and to respond with kindness or help.
- The rich man had everything materially — wealth, comfort, status — but **he lacked the most basic human quality: caring for another human being in need**.
- His failure was not about lacking “spiritual contentment” (he may have felt spiritually fine before death), nor “parental care” (no children are mentioned), nor “a sense of proportion” (though he was excessive, that’s not the core issue).

The parable’s moral is about **compassion, justice, and love for neighbor** — core Christian values. The rich man’s sin was indifference to human suffering.

---

### Final Answer: **human sympathy** ✅

question: In the story of the stilling of the storm, Jesus rebuked
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **the sea and the wind**

---

### Explanation:

The story of **the stilling of the storm** is found in the Gospels — specifically **Mark 4:35–41**, **Matthew 8:23–27**, and **Luke 8:22–25**.

In **Mark 4:39**, it says:

> “He got up, rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Quiet! Be still!’ Then the wind died down and it was completely calm.”

Jesus did **not** rebuke His disciples — though He later *questioned* them about their lack of faith (Mark 4:40: “Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?”), He did not *rebuke* them in the same way He rebuked the storm.

He also did **not** rebuke the devil — while some early Christian interpretations sometimes allegorized the storm as demonic, the text itself does not mention the devil.

So, Jesus **rebuked the sea and the wind** — demonstrating His divine authority over nature.

---

✅ Final Answer: **the sea and the wind**

question: Jesus cured the paralytic man in the city of
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Capernaum**

---

### Explanation:

The story of Jesus healing the paralytic man is recorded in the **Gospel of Mark, chapter 2**, as well as in **Matthew 9:1–8** and **Luke 5:17–26**.

In **Mark 2:1**, it says:

> “When Jesus returned to Capernaum after some days, word spread that he was at home.”

The paralyzed man was brought to Jesus by his friends, who lowered him through the roof because the house was so crowded. Jesus forgave the man’s sins first — which caused controversy among the religious leaders — and then healed him to prove his authority to forgive sins.

> “But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…” He said to the paralytic, “I tell you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.” (Mark 2:10–11)

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Bethlehem**: Jesus was born here, but no major healing miracles are recorded here during his ministry.
- **Nazareth**: Jesus grew up here, but he was rejected by the people there (Luke 4:16–30), and few miracles were performed there during his ministry.
- **Samaria**: This is a region, not a city, and while Jesus interacted with Samaritans (e.g., the woman at the well), the healing of the paralytic did not occur here.

---

### Conclusion:

The healing of the paralytic man took place in **Capernaum**, which was Jesus’ base of operations during much of his Galilean ministry. It was a bustling town on the Sea of Galilee and a center for his teaching and miracles.

✅ So, the correct answer is: **Capernaum**

question: When Jesus uses the phrase "Kingdom of God" in his parables, he means the
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **rule of God**

---

### Explanation:

When Jesus uses the phrase **“Kingdom of God”** (or “Kingdom of Heaven” in Matthew’s Gospel), he is primarily referring to **the active, present, and future reign or rule of God** — not a physical place, but a spiritual reality where God’s will is done, His authority is acknowledged, and His justice and peace are established.

This concept is central to Jesus’ teaching and appears frequently in his parables (e.g., the Parable of the Mustard Seed, the Parable of the Sower, the Parable of the Net). In these stories, Jesus describes the Kingdom as:

- Already present in his ministry and miracles (Luke 17:21 — “the kingdom of God is in your midst”),
- Growing mysteriously and powerfully (Mark 4:26–29),
- Requiring repentance and faith to enter (Mark 1:15),
- And ultimately culminating in the fullness of God’s reign at the end of time.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Judgment Day** — While the Kingdom of God includes final judgment (e.g., the Parable of the Sheep and Goats), judgment is only one aspect, not the primary meaning.
  
- **Firmament** — This is an archaic term for the sky or heavens (from Genesis 1:6–8). It’s not a theological concept Jesus uses to describe his message.

- **Second Coming** — This refers to Christ’s future return, which is related to the *fulfillment* of the Kingdom, but not the meaning of the phrase itself. Jesus often spoke of the Kingdom as *already* breaking into the world through his ministry.

---

### In Summary:

Jesus’ “Kingdom of God” is best understood as **the rule or reign of God** — active now in the hearts of believers and in Jesus’ ministry, and to be fully realized in the future. It’s about God’s sovereign authority being acknowledged and lived out on earth as it is in heaven (Matthew 6:10).

✅ So, the best answer is: **rule of God**.

question: Which of the following signs of Jesus was his last, as recorded by John?
option_d: Raising of Lazarus from the dead
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Raising of Lazarus from the dead**

---

### Explanation:

The Gospel of John records **seven “signs”** (miracles) performed by Jesus, which are meant to reveal His divine identity and mission. These signs are:

1. Turning water into wine at Cana (John 2:1–11)  
2. Healing the official’s son (John 4:46–54)  
3. Healing the man at Bethzatha (John 5:1–15)  
4. Feeding the 5,000 (John 6:1–14)  
5. Walking on water (John 6:16–21)  
6. Healing the man born blind (John 9:1–7)  
7. **Raising Lazarus from the dead** (John 11:1–44)

---

### Why is the raising of Lazarus the *last* sign?

John 11:45–46 notes that **after** this miracle, many believed in Jesus, but the chief priests and Pharisees plotted to kill Him — which directly leads into the events of Passion Week. The raising of Lazarus is the final sign before Jesus’ passion, death, and resurrection.

It’s also the most dramatic and theologically significant sign — it foreshadows Jesus’ own resurrection and demonstrates His power over death. John even says that this miracle was the one that directly led to the decision to kill Jesus (John 11:47–53).

---

### Why not the others?

- **Turning water into wine** — First sign (John 2:11)  
- **Feeding the multitude** — Fourth sign (John 6:1–14)  
- **Healing at Bethzatha** — Third sign (John 5:1–15)  

So, **raising Lazarus** is chronologically and thematically the last of the seven signs in John’s Gospel.

---

✅ Final Answer: **Raising of Lazarus from the dead**

question: The appearance of Moses and Elijah during the Transfiguration was to
option_a: congratulate Jesus on the success of his ministry
option_b: confirm their legal and prophetic roles
option_c: assure Jesus of victory over his enemies
option_d: settle down with Jesus in glory
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **confirm their legal and prophetic roles**

---

### Explanation:

The **Transfiguration** is described in the Gospels (Matthew 17:1–8, Mark 9:2–8, Luke 9:28–36). During this event, Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, and **Moses and Elijah appear and talk with Him**.

- **Moses** represents the **Law** (Torah), as he received the Ten Commandments and led Israel under the covenant.
- **Elijah** represents the **Prophets**, as he was one of the greatest prophets in the Old Testament and was taken to heaven without dying.

Their presence together with Jesus on the mountain symbolizes the **fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets in Jesus** (see Matthew 5:17). They are not there to congratulate Jesus, assure Him of victory, or settle down with Him — those are not the theological or narrative purposes of the scene.

Instead, their appearance serves to **confirm Jesus’ divine mission and authority** by showing that He is the culmination of the Old Testament — the one to whom the Law and the Prophets point.

Additionally, in Luke 9:31, it says they spoke with Jesus about **“his departure, which he was about to bring to fulfillment at Jerusalem”** — that is, His death and resurrection. This further underscores that their role was to affirm Jesus’ mission, not to celebrate or settle down.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Congratulate Jesus on the success of his ministry** — Jesus’ ministry was not yet complete; He was heading toward the cross. No congratulation is implied.
- **Assure Jesus of victory over his enemies** — While Jesus’ victory is implied, the text doesn’t say Moses and Elijah were there for this purpose.
- **Settle down with Jesus in glory** — Peter even suggests building shelters (tents) to stay, but God interrupts and says, “This is my Son, listen to him” — emphasizing obedience, not settling down.

---

### Conclusion:

The appearance of Moses and Elijah was to **confirm their legal and prophetic roles** — and to show that Jesus is the fulfillment of both.

✅ Correct Answer: **confirm their legal and prophetic roles**

question: The miracles of Jesus recorded in John's Gospel are called
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **signs of Jesus**

---

### Explanation:

In the Gospel of John, the miracles performed by Jesus are consistently referred to as **“signs”** (Greek: *semeia* — σημεῖα). This is a deliberate theological choice by the author to emphasize that these miracles are not merely displays of power or wonders for entertainment, but **meaningful acts that point to Jesus’ divine identity and mission**.

John uses the term “sign” to highlight that each miracle reveals something about who Jesus is — the Son of God, the Messiah, the Word made flesh. These signs are meant to evoke faith in those who witness or hear about them.

For example:
- The turning of water into wine at Cana (John 2:11) is called “the first of his signs,” and it “revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.”
- The healing of the official’s son (John 4:54) is called “the second sign.”
- The feeding of the 5,000 (John 6:14) points to Jesus as the Bread of Life.
- The raising of Lazarus (John 11:45–46) is the climactic sign that leads to increased belief — and also to the decision to kill Jesus.

John’s Gospel concludes by stating:
> “Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not recorded in this book. But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:30–31)

This underscores the **purpose** of the signs: to lead people to faith.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Wonders of Jesus** — While the miracles are indeed wondrous, this term is not used in John’s Gospel as the theological label for them.
- **Gifts of Jesus** — This is more associated with spiritual gifts (e.g., in 1 Corinthians 12) or grace, not the miracles themselves.
- **Demonstrations of Jesus** — Too vague and not a biblical or theological term used in John.

---

### Conclusion:

The miracles in John’s Gospel are called **“signs of Jesus”** because they are divine indicators pointing to his identity and mission — meant to provoke faith and understanding.

✅ Correct Answer: **signs of Jesus**

question: By raising Lazarus to life, Jesus shows his
option_b: redemptive power to raise man to eternal life
option_d: Messiahship to the people of Bethany
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **redemptive power to raise man to eternal life**

---

### Explanation:

The raising of Lazarus from the dead (recorded in **John 11**) is one of the most dramatic and theologically significant miracles in the Gospel of John. Jesus deliberately delays going to Bethany after hearing that Lazarus is ill, and by the time He arrives, Lazarus has been dead for four days. Jesus then calls Lazarus forth from the tomb, and he comes out alive.

This miracle is not merely a display of compassion (though Jesus does weep with Mary and Martha — John 11:35), nor is it primarily about forgiving sins (though Jesus does claim authority to forgive sins elsewhere, e.g., Mark 2:5–12). It is also not *only* about revealing His Messiahship to the people of Bethany — though it does confirm His identity.

Rather, **John presents this miracle as a sign pointing to Jesus’ authority over death itself — a foreshadowing of His own resurrection and a demonstration of His power to grant eternal life**.

Jesus Himself says in John 11:25–26:

> “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die; and whoever lives by believing in me will never die. Do you believe this?”

This is the theological heart of the story. Jesus is showing that **He has the redemptive power to raise the dead to eternal life** — not just temporarily, as Lazarus was raised to die again later, but ultimately, as Jesus Himself would rise and grant eternal life to believers.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Power to forgive sins** — This is demonstrated in other miracles (e.g., the paralytic in Mark 2), but not the focus here.
- **Sympathy for Martha and Mary** — Jesus does show compassion (He weeps), but that’s not the *primary theological point* of the miracle.
- **Messiahship to the people of Bethany** — While it does confirm His identity, John’s Gospel emphasizes the *cosmic and eternal significance* of this sign — pointing to Jesus as the source of resurrection and life.

---

### Conclusion:

Jesus raising Lazarus is a powerful demonstration of His **redemptive power to raise man to eternal life** — a key theme in John’s Gospel and foundational to Christian hope in resurrection.

✅ Final Answer: **redemptive power to raise man to eternal life**

question: According to St. Mark, Mary Magdalene and the other women went to the tomb but did not see
option_b: a young man dressed in white
step_by_step:
According to **St. Mark’s Gospel (Mark 16:1–8)**, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome went to the tomb early on the first day of the week to anoint Jesus’ body. When they arrived, they found:

- **The stone already rolled away** (Mark 16:4) — they saw this.
- **An empty tomb** (Mark 16:5) — they saw the tomb was empty.
- **A young man dressed in white** sitting inside (Mark 16:5) — they saw him and were terrified.

But **they did NOT see Jesus of Nazareth**.

The young man (an angel) told them:  
> “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’” (Mark 16:6–7)

So, while they saw the evidence of the resurrection — the rolled-away stone, the empty tomb, and the angel — **they did not see the risen Jesus himself**.

---

✅ **Correct Answer: Jesus of Nazareth**

---

**Explanation Summary:**
Mark’s account ends with the women fleeing in fear and saying nothing to anyone (Mark 16:8), implying they did not encounter the risen Christ at the tomb. The appearances of Jesus to the disciples occur later in the Gospel (in the longer ending, Mark 16:9–20, which many scholars believe was added later). But in the original ending (Mark 16:8), **Jesus is not seen** by the women at the tomb.

Thus, according to **St. Mark’s Gospel**, the women saw the stone rolled away, the empty tomb, and the young man in white — but **not Jesus of Nazareth**.

question: The early church showed that it was not prepared to condone the sin of hypocrisy and greed with the story of
option_b: Saul on the road to Damascus
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Ananias and Sapphira**

---

### Explanation:

The story of **Ananias and Sapphira** (Acts 5:1–11) is a powerful example in the early church of how seriously the apostles and the Christian community took **hypocrisy and greed** — sins that directly contradicted the spirit of generosity and sincerity that marked the early church.

#### What happened:
- Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a piece of property.
- They agreed to give the proceeds to the apostles (as many believers were doing — see Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–37).
- But they **kept part of the money for themselves** while **pretending** to give it all — essentially lying to the Holy Spirit and the church.
- Peter confronted Ananias, who fell down and died immediately. Later, Sapphira, when questioned, also lied and suffered the same fate.

#### Why this matters:
- The story demonstrates that the **early church was not willing to tolerate hypocrisy or greed**, even among its own members.
- Peter’s words make it clear: they weren’t just lying to people — they were lying to God (Acts 5:4).
- The result was **fear and awe** in the church, reinforcing the seriousness of integrity and sincerity in the Christian community.

---

### Why not the others?

- **Appointment of Matthias** (Acts 1:21–26): This was about replacing Judas — a matter of leadership and continuity, not hypocrisy or greed.
- **Saul on the road to Damascus** (Acts 9): This is about conversion and repentance — Saul was a persecutor, not a hypocrite within the church.
- **Elymas, the magician at Paphos** (Acts 13:6–12): He was an opponent of the gospel, trying to turn a proconsul away from faith. He was struck blind — but this was about **opposing the truth**, not hypocrisy or greed within the church.

---

### Conclusion:
The story of **Ananias and Sapphira** is the clearest and most direct example in the New Testament of the early church’s refusal to condone **hypocrisy and greed** — making it the correct answer.

✅ Final Answer: **Ananias and Sapphira**

question: From his experience on the road to Damascus, Saul learnt all the following except that
option_a: to persecute the church meant persecuting the Lord
option_b: his confidence in Judaism was misplaced
option_c: he was specially chosen to preach to the Gentiles
option_d: he would successfully promote his own will
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **he would successfully promote his own will**

---

### Explanation:

The **road to Damascus** experience (recorded in Acts 9, 22, and 26) was the dramatic conversion of **Saul (later Paul)** from a zealous persecutor of Christians to a devoted follower of Jesus Christ. During this encounter, Jesus appeared to Saul in a blinding light and spoke to him directly.

Let’s examine each option:

---

✅ **“To persecute the church meant persecuting the Lord”**  
— This is directly stated by Jesus in Acts 9:4-5:  
> *“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”*  
Jesus identifies Himself with His church — to persecute believers is to persecute Him. So Saul learned this.

---

✅ **“His confidence in Judaism was misplaced”**  
— Saul was a Pharisee, zealous for the law (Philippians 3:5-6). His encounter with Christ revealed that his zeal was misdirected — he had been opposing God’s true plan. He later writes in Philippians 3:7-8 that he counted everything as loss for the sake of Christ. So yes, he learned his confidence in Judaism (as he understood it) was misplaced.

---

✅ **“He was specially chosen to preach to the Gentiles”**  
— Jesus tells Ananias in Acts 9:15:  
> *“Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel.”*  
Paul himself affirms this calling repeatedly (e.g., Romans 11:13, Galatians 2:7-8). So this was part of his revelation.

---

❌ **“He would successfully promote his own will”**  
— This is **not** what Saul learned. In fact, the opposite is true. His conversion involved **surrendering his own will** to Christ’s. He was blinded, humbled, and told to go where he was commanded — not to follow his own plans. His life became one of obedience, suffering, and submission to God’s will (e.g., Acts 20:22-24, 2 Corinthians 12:7-10).

Paul even says in Galatians 2:20:  
> *“I have been crucified with Christ and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me.”*

So, promoting his *own will* is contrary to everything he learned on the road to Damascus.

---

### ✅ Final Answer: **he would successfully promote his own will**  
*(This is the exception — the thing he did NOT learn.)*

question: Another name for Tabitha who was raised from the dead was
step_by_step:
The correct answer is **Dorcas**.

**Explanation:**

In the New Testament, specifically in the Book of Acts (9:36-42), a disciple in Joppa named **Tabitha** (an Aramaic name) is raised from the dead by the Apostle Peter. The text immediately notes that "Tabitha" is translated as **Dorcas** (the Greek equivalent). Both names mean "gazelle."

**Why the others are incorrect:**

*   **Mary Magdalene**: A different follower of Jesus from Magdala.
*   **Joanna**: A different woman who was a follower and benefactor of Jesus (mentioned in Luke 8:3 and 24:10).
*   **Aeneas**: A paralytic man healed by Peter in Lydda (Acts 9:32-35), not another name for Tabitha.

question: The delegation from Antioch to the Council of Jerusalem comprised
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Paul and Barnabas**

---

### Explanation:

The **Council of Jerusalem** (recorded in **Acts 15**) was a pivotal early church meeting held around 49–50 AD to address whether Gentile converts to Christianity needed to follow Jewish customs, especially circumcision.

According to **Acts 15:2**, the church in Antioch (where Paul and Barnabas had been ministering) decided to send **Paul and Barnabas** to Jerusalem to consult with the apostles and elders about this issue.

> **Acts 15:2 (NIV):**  
> *“After Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question.”*

They were **delegates from Antioch**, representing the Gentile mission and the church there. Peter and James were **leaders in Jerusalem** — Peter was one of the original apostles, and James (the brother of Jesus) was the leader of the Jerusalem church. They were not delegates *from Antioch*; they were the ones receiving the delegation.

---

### Why the other options are incorrect:

- **Paul and Peter**: Peter was not from Antioch; he was a Jerusalem apostle (though he later visited Antioch — Galatians 2:11).
- **Peter and James**: Both were Jerusalem leaders, not delegates from Antioch.
- **Barnabas and James**: James was not from Antioch — he was the Jerusalem church leader.

---

### Conclusion:

The delegation **from Antioch** to the Council of Jerusalem was **Paul and Barnabas** — they were sent to represent the Gentile mission and the Antioch church’s position.

✅ Correct Answer: **Paul and Barnabas**

question: Paul said that Jesus died for us while we were yet sinners in order to
option_a: Prove that he was not an ordinary man
option_b: show God's love for sinful man
option_c: warns us to desist from sin
option_d: give us power to possess the earth
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **show God's love for sinful man**

---

**Explanation:**

This statement comes from **Romans 5:8** in the New Testament:

> “But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (NIV)

Paul is emphasizing the **unconditional and sacrificial nature of God’s love**. He is not saying Jesus died *after* we cleaned up our lives or became righteous — but **while we were still sinners**, meaning unworthy, rebellious, and separated from God.

This highlights that **God’s love is主动 (initiative), gracious, and undeserved** — it’s not based on our merit, but on His mercy and desire to reconcile us to Himself.

---

**Why not the other options?**

- **Prove that he was not an ordinary man** — While Jesus’ death and resurrection do demonstrate His divinity, Paul’s point here is not to prove Jesus’ identity, but to reveal the *depth of God’s love*.

- **Warns us to desist from sin** — Paul does warn against sin elsewhere (e.g., Romans 6), but in Romans 5:8, the focus is on *God’s love*, not a warning.

- **Give us power to possess the earth** — This is not a biblical theme connected to Jesus’ death in this context. The “possessing the earth” idea is more related to Genesis or eschatological promises, not Romans 5:8.

---

✅ So, the best and most accurate answer is: **show God's love for sinful man**.

question: "As one man's trespass led to the condemnation for all men, so one man's act of righteousness leads to acquittal and life for all men". The two men involved here are
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Adam and Jesus Christ**

---

### Explanation:

This quote is a direct reference to **Romans 5:18** in the New Testament:

> *“Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men.”* (ESV)

This verse is part of Paul’s theological argument in Romans 5, where he contrasts **Adam** and **Jesus Christ** as two representative figures — or “federal heads” — of humanity.

---

### Breakdown:

- **Adam’s trespass (sin)** — When Adam disobeyed God in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 3), his sin brought **condemnation and death** to all humanity. Paul says “sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and in this way death came to all people, because all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

- **Jesus Christ’s act of righteousness** — Jesus’ perfect obedience, culminating in His sacrificial death and resurrection, brings **justification (acquittal) and eternal life** to all who believe. Paul calls Jesus the “last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45) — the one who reverses the curse of the first Adam.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **Moses and Abraham** — Important patriarchs and leaders, but not the two representative figures in this theological contrast.
- **Esau and Jacob** — Brothers in Genesis, involved in a story of inheritance and blessing, not a universal theological contrast of sin and redemption.
- **Cain and Abel** — The first murder story; illustrates sin’s consequences, but not representative of all humanity in the way Adam and Christ are.

---

### Theological Significance:

This contrast is foundational to Christian theology — **original sin** (through Adam) and **salvation through Christ** (the “second Adam”). It shows that just as humanity fell through one man’s disobedience, redemption comes through one man’s obedience.

---

✅ So, the two men involved are: **Adam and Jesus Christ**.

question: When Paul admonished Christians to set their minds on things that are above, he wanted them to concentrate on the
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **will and purposes of God**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to **Colossians 3:1–2**, where the Apostle Paul writes:

> *“If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.”* (ESV)

Paul is urging believers to **fix their thoughts and priorities on spiritual realities** — specifically, on **Christ and His heavenly realm** — rather than being consumed by earthly, temporary, or worldly concerns.

Let’s evaluate the options:

- **Things they dream about** — This is too vague and subjective. Paul is not encouraging daydreaming or personal fantasies.
  
- **Necessities of life** — Paul actually acknowledges these in other passages (e.g., Philippians 4:19), but here he’s calling believers to **transcend** earthly concerns, not focus on them.

- **Will and purposes of God** — ✅ This is the best answer. “Things that are above” refers to **God’s eternal plan, Christ’s reign, spiritual realities, and living according to God’s will**. Paul wants believers to align their thinking and living with God’s heavenly perspective.

- **Imminent coming of our Lord** — While this is a biblical theme (e.g., 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18), it’s not the primary focus of Colossians 3:1–2. Paul is speaking more broadly about **mindset and spiritual orientation**, not specifically eschatology.

---

### Conclusion:

Paul’s call to “set your minds on things that are above” is a call to **live with a heavenly perspective**, centered on **God’s will and purposes** — not earthly distractions or personal whims. Therefore, the correct answer is:

> **will and purposes of God** ✅

question: Paul's example of humility in his Epistle to the Philippians is
option_a: Jesus taking the form of a servant
option_c: reckoning what is best for oneself
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **Jesus taking the form of a servant**

---

**Explanation:**

In the **Epistle to the Philippians**, specifically in **Philippians 2:5–8**, Paul presents **Jesus Christ** as the supreme example of humility. He writes:

> “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.” (ESV)

Paul uses Jesus’ self-emptying (kenosis) and His willingness to take on the role of a servant — even to the point of death — as the model for Christian humility. He urges believers to have the same mindset: putting others before themselves, not seeking personal glory, but serving with humility.

---

**Why the other options are incorrect:**

- **Counting oneself superior to others** — This is the *opposite* of humility. Paul explicitly warns against this in Philippians 2:3: “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves.”

- **Reckoning what is best for oneself** — Again, this reflects self-centeredness, not humility. Paul’s ethic is others-centered.

- **Jesus rising up in glory** — While true that Jesus was exalted (Phil. 2:9–11), Paul presents this as the *result* of His humility, not the example itself. The *example* is His humble descent, not His glorious ascent.

---

✅ So, the example of humility Paul gives is **Jesus taking the form of a servant** — a radical act of self-giving love and obedience.

question: Commenting on the date of the parousia, Paul advised the Thessalonians to
option_a: be sober in maintaining their hope of salvation
option_c: know that the date will be announced later
option_d: enjoy peace and security in the face of danger
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **be sober in maintaining their hope of salvation**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to Paul’s letter to the **Thessalonians**, particularly **1 Thessalonians 5:1–11**, where Paul addresses concerns about the **parousia** (the second coming of Christ). The Thessalonians were anxious and possibly confused about when Christ would return — some may have even stopped working, expecting His immediate return.

In **1 Thessalonians 5:1–3**, Paul says:

> “Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying, ‘There is peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them…”

Paul is **not** saying to ignore the topic or that the date will be announced later. Instead, he **warns against speculation** and **urges readiness** — not by calculating dates, but by living faithfully and soberly.

In **1 Thessalonians 5:6–8**, he writes:

> “So then let us not sleep, as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, are drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, and put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation.”

Here, “**be sober**” is a metaphor for spiritual alertness, self-control, and readiness — not drunkenness or complacency. Paul encourages them to **maintain their hope of salvation** by living responsibly and faithfully, **without being consumed by speculation** about the timing of Christ’s return.

---

### Why not the other options?

- **“Disregard all speculations about it”** — While Paul does discourage date-setting, he doesn’t say to disregard *all* speculation. He addresses their fears and gives theological grounding. He wants them to be informed and prepared, not ignorant.

- **“Know that the date will be announced later”** — Paul explicitly says **no one knows the day or hour** (cf. Mark 13:32), and he doesn’t promise future announcements.

- **“Enjoy peace and security in the face of danger”** — Paul actually warns that people will say “peace and security” right before sudden destruction comes (1 Thess 5:3). He’s cautioning *against* complacency, not encouraging it.

---

### Conclusion:

Paul’s pastoral advice is to **live soberly, alertly, and faithfully**, holding fast to the **hope of salvation** — not to obsess over dates or fall into false security. Thus, the best answer is:

> **be sober in maintaining their hope of salvation** ✅

question: Paul was so confident in his epistle to Philemon that the letter would grant his major request because
option_a: Philemon was a Roman citizen like Paul
option_b: they were from the same town
option_c: they were partners in the faith of Christ
option_d: Philemon had expected such a request
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **they were partners in the faith of Christ**

---

**Explanation:**

In the **Epistle to Philemon**, Paul writes a personal, heartfelt letter to Philemon, a Christian believer and a leader in the Colossian church. Paul is appealing to Philemon to welcome back **Onesimus**, a runaway slave who had become a Christian under Paul’s influence. Paul asks Philemon not only to receive Onesimus but to receive him “no longer as a slave but better than a slave — as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16).

Paul expresses great confidence that Philemon will comply with his request. He writes:

> “I am confident in you — I know that you will do even more than I ask.” (Philemon 1:21, NIV)

Why is Paul so confident?

He doesn’t base his confidence on legal status (Philemon was not necessarily a Roman citizen — and even if he were, that’s not mentioned), nor on shared geography (they weren’t from the same town — Paul was from Tarsus, Philemon from Colossae), nor on Philemon anticipating the request (there’s no indication Philemon expected this).

Instead, Paul bases his confidence on their **shared faith in Christ** and their **spiritual partnership**. Paul refers to Philemon as:

> “our dear friend and fellow worker” (Philemon 1:1)  
> “fellow soldier” (Philemon 1:2)  
> “partner” (Philemon 1:17)

This language emphasizes their **mutual commitment to the gospel**, their **brotherhood in Christ**, and their **spiritual unity**. Paul is confident because he knows Philemon’s character — his love, his faith, and his willingness to act in accordance with Christian principles.

Thus, the best answer is: **they were partners in the faith of Christ** — this is the foundation of Paul’s confidence.

---

✅ Final Answer: **they were partners in the faith of Christ**

question: In his letter to Philemon, Paul did not specifically ask him to
option_a: grant freedom to his slave Onesimus
option_b: allow Onesimus to become a servant of God
option_c: forgive Onesimus for his earlier behaviour
option_d: prepare a guest room for him
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **grant freedom to his slave Onesimus**

---

### Explanation:

In the **Letter to Philemon**, the Apostle Paul writes a personal and heartfelt appeal on behalf of **Onesimus**, a runaway slave who had become a Christian under Paul’s influence. Paul sends Onesimus back to his master, Philemon, and asks Philemon to receive him not as a slave, but as a **beloved brother in Christ** (Philemon 1:16).

However, **Paul does not explicitly command or even directly ask Philemon to free Onesimus**. Instead, he appeals to Philemon’s love, faith, and Christian conscience. He says:

> “Perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother…” (Philemon 1:15–16, ESV)

Paul also says:

> “I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart… I would have liked to keep him with me… but I preferred to do nothing without your consent…” (Philemon 1:12, 13, 14)

This shows Paul’s **deliberate restraint** — he does not command Philemon to free Onesimus, even though he implies that it would be the Christian thing to do. He leaves the decision to Philemon’s own volition, appealing to grace and brotherly love rather than authority.

---

### Why the other options are incorrect:

- **Allow Onesimus to become a servant of God** — Paul *does* imply this, since Onesimus is now a Christian and Paul calls him “my very heart” and “a beloved brother.” So this is *not* what Paul *didn’t* ask.

- **Forgive Onesimus for his earlier behaviour** — Paul *does* ask for forgiveness. He says, “If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account” (Philemon 1:18). So this is explicitly requested.

- **Prepare a guest room for him** — Paul *does* ask this at the end: “Prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be granted to you” (Philemon 1:22). So this is also requested.

---

### Conclusion:

Paul **did not specifically ask** Philemon to **grant freedom to his slave Onesimus**, even though he strongly implies it would be the loving, Christian response. He leaves that decision to Philemon’s conscience — which is precisely why this letter is so remarkable for its pastoral sensitivity and respect for human agency.

✅ So, the correct answer is: **grant freedom to his slave Onesimus**.

question: James taught that religion that is pure and undefiled before God is shown by
option_b: loving the needy and purity of life
option_d: taking part in all the activities in the church
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **loving the needy and purity of life**

---

### Explanation:

This question refers to **James 1:27** in the Bible, which says:

> “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.”  
> — **James 1:27 (ESV)**

This verse defines what true, genuine religion looks like in God’s eyes — not merely rituals or religious activities, but **practical compassion** (visiting/caring for the vulnerable — orphans and widows) and **personal moral purity** (keeping oneself unstained from the world).

---

### Why the other options are incorrect:

- **Reading the Bible** — While valuable and important, James is emphasizing *action* and *lifestyle*, not just study or devotionals.
- **Preaching the word of God** — Also important, but not the definition James gives here for “pure and undefiled religion.”
- **Taking part in all the activities in the church** — James is critiquing empty religiosity; mere church attendance or activity without genuine love and holiness is not what he means by “pure religion.”

---

### In summary:

James defines true religion as **active love for the needy** and **personal holiness** — a faith that works itself out in deeds of mercy and moral integrity.

✅ So, the best answer is: **loving the needy and purity of life**.

question: During the second coming of Jesus, surviving Christians would
option_a: reign forever on earth with Him
option_b: join the happy throng to meet Him in the clouds
option_c: occupy a minor position in heaven after after those who had previously died
option_d: join in fighting against the anti christ
step_by_step:
The correct answer is: **join the happy throng to meet Him in the clouds**

---

### Explanation:
